summary: Defines a standard set of field names, called the Electronic Commerce Modeling Language version 1.1, for the information that online merchants ask customers to type in. With common fields, wallet software can fill in forms automatically, and manual entry is less confusing too.

eli5.summary: Every shop asks for your name and address in a different order. This gives all shops the same form so a helper can fill it out for you.

questions: standard fields for online checkout forms
ecml field names for online checkout
subtitle: A shared set of field names for online checkout forms, so wallet software can fill them in for you.

tldr.problem: Every online merchant used different form fields for names, addresses and card details, which confused customers and made checkout tedious. The RFC reports that around two thirds of merchant forms were abandoned during fill in.
tldr.mechanism: ECML 1.1 defines a standard list of field names, such as Ecom_Payment_Card_Number, plus a few fields for merchant-to-customer messages. The names can be used in HTML forms or an XML encoding, so electronic wallets from different vendors can fill them in.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes ECML 1.0 (RFC 2706) and has been updated by RFC 4112. It only names fields; it adds no payment technology and does not replace TLS, SET or IOTP.

today: RFC 3106 is Informational. It obsoletes RFC 2706 (ECML 1.0) and has been updated by RFC 4112. Its own IESG note says ECML version 2.0 was under development in the IETF TRADE Working Group at publication.

sections.title: Why Standard Checkout Fields
sections.content:
Merchants were already taking orders through HTML forms, but the data formats varied a lot from one merchant to the next. Users found this confusing and manual entry tedious. The RFC says reportedly around two thirds of merchant forms were abandoned part way through.

An electronic wallet is an application or service that stores billing, shipping, payment and preference information and uses it to complete merchant forms automatically. Wallets had been built many ways, for example into browsers, as proxy servers or as plug-ins, but the lack of standards hampered them. The Electronic Commerce Modeling Language (ECML) is a set of simple guidelines for merchants that lets wallets from multiple vendors fill in their forms.

The fields come from the ECML Alliance, whose Steering Committee has fifteen members. Version 1.1 improves on version 1.0 (RFC 2706), which it obsoletes, mainly by adding merchant-to-wallet communication. ECML is described as an open standard that needs no license and adds no new technology to the web.
sections.eli5: Imagine every shop in town had a different order slip, so you wrote your address again and again. ECML makes all the slips look the same, so a helper can write it for you.

sections.title: The Field List
sections.content:
The ECML standard is mainly the definition and naming of fields. Names are hierarchical, built with underscores, such as Ecom_ShipTo_Postal_Name_First. This lets a protocol request or send a whole aggregate, for example Ecom_ShipTo for everything the customer will provide about where to ship.

Customer-to-merchant fields cover three parties: ShipTo, BillTo and ReceiptTo. Each has name parts, company, three street lines, city, state or province, postal code, country, phone and email. ReceiptTo is for cases such as corporate purchasing cards, where the individual card holder is in ReceiptTo and the corporate owner is in BillTo. Payment fields include Ecom_Payment_Card_Name, _Type, _Number, _Verification, expiry day, month and year, and _Protocol. Other fields carry the order ID, a user ID and password for an existing merchant account, the schema version and a wallet ID.

The Min column in the table is the minimum data size to allow on entry, not the minimum size of a valid value. For example the card number field has a Min of 19, the longest number the ISO standard permits, and the postal code has 14, believed to be the maximum needed anywhere. Merchants must accept longer or shorter values where needed.

Some footnotes give value rules: address lines must be filled in the order line1, line2, line3; country uses two-letter ISO 3166 codes; card type uses the first 4 letters of the association name, such as VISA, MAST or AMER; and the card protocol field is a space-separated list of tokens such as none, set, setcert, iotp, echeck, simcard and phoneid.
sections.eli5: The form has labelled boxes: first name, street, card number and so on. Every shop uses the same label for the same box, so the helper knows what goes where.

sections.title: Merchant-to-Wallet Fields and Encodings
sections.content:
A second group of fields flows from the merchant to the consumer's software. They are usually hidden fields: Ecom_Merchant, Ecom_Processor, Ecom_Transaction_ID, Ecom_Transaction_Inquiry (a URL for asking about the transaction), Ecom_Transaction_Amount, a currency code (for example USD), a date, a type (debit or credit, if known) and a signature. The format of the receipt signatures is not specified in this document.

ECML defines names, not a single wire format. The normal use in HTML is a form whose input field names match the list, and INPUT tags of type text, hidden and password must be supported, as must SELECT tags. The RFC also gives an XML DTD, with elements such as ShipTo, BillTo, Payment and Transaction. For XML, the general XML character encoding rules apply, which mandate support of UTF-8 and UTF-16, and the xml:lang attribute can carry language information.
sections.eli5: After you buy, the shop can quietly hand your helper a receipt with the order number, the price and the date.

sections.title: Using the Fields
sections.content:
To conform, field names must be structured and named as close to the listed structure as the transaction protocol allows. The labels users see are not restricted.

Merchants choose which fields to ask for, and when. They may ask for ship-to details first so shipping cost can be computed before payment details. Version 1.0 and 1.1 have no way to say which fields are mandatory, so for customer software every field is optional, though a merchant may show an error or ask again.

Two fields manage the flow. Ecom_SchemaVersion is REQUIRED on every web page that has any Ecom fields, and it is recommended to be the last Ecom field on the page so a wallet can tell when it can stop filling. Its value for this version is http://www.ecml.org/version/1.1. Ecom_TransactionComplete should appear on the last page of a transaction, just before the schema version field, so multi-page fill logic knows when to stop. Because some wallets need user activation, there should also be at least one user-visible Ecom field on every such page.
sections.eli5: A hidden sticker on each page tells the helper which form style is used. Another sticker on the last page says the order is finished, so the helper stops.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The fields hold sensitive data, so they should be secured when sent over the public Internet or any observable channel. The RFC does not specify the protection but says channel encryption such as TLS/SSL (RFC 2246) or IPSec (RFC 2411) would be appropriate in many cases.

Users need control over the release of the information. A wallet on a shared or public terminal should be configurable so that its memory of addresses and contact details is fully disabled, which the RFC calls vital for library patrons, students, customers at public terminals and children. Stored contact information should be protectable with a password, and automated multi-page fill should stop when it sees Ecom_TransactionComplete until fill is authorized again.
sections.eli5: Your address and card number are private, so send them in a locked box. A helper on a shared computer should forget them, and stop when the order is done.
